qEBJxZS5NrM.title: Preparing for Ramadan 2: The Five Treasures of Ramadan
qEBJxZS5NrM.one_line: Using the hadith of Salman al-Farisi, he lays out five treasures of Ramadan: forgiveness, release from the Fire, multiplied rewards, answered dua and Laylat al-Qadr.
qEBJxZS5NrM.summary: The second preparatory session for Ramadan opens with the long hadith of Salman al-Farisi about the coming month, which he accepts for its meanings while noting the weakness of its chain. He frames the session in two parts, treasures and planning, and argues that intention in Islam is real planning backed by resolve, not a wish. He then sets out five treasures. First, forgiveness of sins: a believer feels sins as a mountain, and Ramadan offers forgiveness through fasting, night prayer or the last ten nights, with an ease that only Hajj matches. Second, release from the Fire, which Allah grants each night according to effort, and which the Prophet sought above all. Third, multiplied rewards: a voluntary act equals an obligation, an obligation equals seventy, fasting's reward is beyond counting, yet a fast that abstains from the lawful while indulging the unlawful is hollow. Fourth, answered dua: Allah removed every intermediary in 2:186 and wants to hear His servant, and He fills mosques even in a small Canadian city. Fifth, Laylat al-Qadr, a night worth a lifetime, hidden in the last ten so that only those who strive reach it. He asks listeners to prepare their duas, guard their fasts and enter the month with a plan.

outline.heading: Opening
The hadith of Salman al-Farisi on Ramadan
outline.gist: He reads the hadith about the coming great month, explaining that its chain is weak but its meanings are supported elsewhere.

outline.heading: Intention as planning
outline.gist: The session has two parts, treasures and planning; intention in Islam is a plan backed by resolve, not a passing wish.

outline.heading: Treasure one: forgiveness and the weight of sin
outline.gist: A believer feels his sins like a mountain over him, unlike the hypocrite who brushes them off like a fly.

outline.heading: Forgiveness through fasting, standing and the last ten
outline.gist: Three routes to forgiveness in Ramadan, and the Prophet's warning for one who leaves Ramadan unforgiven.

outline.heading: Ramadan's ease compared to Hajj
outline.gist: Only an accepted Hajj gives a comparable reward, yet Ramadan asks far less: fasting at home and praying in congregation.

outline.heading: Treasure two: the terror of the Fire
outline.gist: Nations kneel before Hell and the criminal would ransom his children, family and all on earth to escape it.

outline.heading: Release from the Fire is earned by effort
outline.gist: Allah frees people every night and more in the last ten, choosing them by their striving; once freed He keeps returning them to Him.

outline.heading: The Prophet's constant plea for release
outline.gist: Across his nine Ramadans the Prophet asked for nothing more than release from the Fire.

outline.heading: Treasure three: a voluntary act worth an obligation
outline.gist: Nothing equals an obligatory act, so a nafl valued as a fard is a great gift; taraweeh is a search for Allah's love through voluntary acts.

outline.heading: A day broken without excuse cannot be recovered
outline.gist: The sick must break their fast and pay fidyah, but a healthy person who breaks a fast without excuse can make it up yet never regain its reward.

outline.heading: Fasting has no fixed price
outline.gist: Every deed has a value on the Day of Judgment except fasting, whose reward Allah keeps for Himself.

outline.heading: Fear of rejected deeds: quality or quantity
outline.gist: Many fast and gain only hunger; if your deeds lack quality, at least have quantity, but never come with neither.

outline.heading: Abstaining from the lawful while committing the unlawful
outline.gist: A fast includes the eyes, ears, mind and limbs; saying 'I am fasting' reminds the self, and it makes no sense to give up food yet indulge in haram.

outline.heading: Treasure four: dua with no intermediary
outline.gist: In 2:186 Allah answers directly without the usual 'say', speaking to the servant without even the Prophet in between.

outline.heading: Allah wants to hear your problems
outline.gist: No creature truly wants to hear your troubles, yet Allah commands you to call on Him and ties refusing dua to arrogance.

outline.heading: Allah calls hearts to the mosques
outline.gist: On the first night of Ramadan mosques fill across the world, even in a small Canadian city; it is Allah who brings people, and the best servant makes them love Him.

outline.heading: The fasting person's dua and what acceptance means
outline.gist: The dua at iftar is not rejected; acceptance means Allah gives what you asked, something better, or averts a harm.

outline.heading: The companions prepared their duas for months
outline.gist: They wrote and memorized duas before Ramadan and used every prostration and pre-dawn hour.

outline.heading: Treasure five: Laylat al-Qadr, a night better than a lifetime
outline.gist: Qadr means standing and rank; the night of the Quran's descent outweighs a thousand months, about a whole human life.

outline.heading: Life is measured by what it changes
outline.gist: Thousands of ordinary nights could be erased without effect, while the one night of revelation changed human history; what is your own night of qadr?

outline.heading: Hidden in the last ten to demand effort
outline.gist: Nothing of worth is reached without sacrifice, so the night is concealed to make you strive every night.

outline.heading: Jibril descends to inspect the Quran
outline.gist: Angels descend that night to see what Muslims have done with the Quran; seek repentance rather than signs and visions.

outline.heading: The scale tipped by one night
outline.gist: Every deed that night weighs as though done for 83 years, tipping the scale toward good.

outline.heading: Compensation for short lives
outline.gist: Companions often died young and asked how they could match earlier nations; Laylat al-Qadr gives a lifetime each year.

outline.heading: Recap and a sixth treasure: Allah boasts to the angels
outline.gist: He lists the five treasures; some scholars add Allah's pride before the angels in His hungry, thirsty servants.

outline.heading: Outro

2:183.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ كُتِبَ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَتَّقُونَ
2:183.en: O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)

2:184.ar: أَيَّامࣰ ا مَّعۡدُودَٰتࣲۚ فَمَن كَانَ مِنكُم مَّرِيضًا أَوۡ عَلَىٰ سَفَرࣲ فَعِدَّةࣱ مِّنۡ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَۚ وَعَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُۥ فِدۡيَةࣱ طَعَامُ مِسۡكِينࣲۖ فَمَن تَطَوَّعَ خَيۡرࣰ ا فَهُوَ خَيۡرࣱ لَّهُۥۚ وَأَن تَصُومُواْ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ

2:185.ar: شَهۡرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ هُدࣰ ى لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَٰتࣲ مِّنَ ٱلۡهُدَىٰ وَٱلۡفُرۡقَانِۚ فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ ٱلشَّهۡرَ فَلۡيَصُمۡهُۖ وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوۡ عَلَىٰ سَفَرࣲ فَعِدَّةࣱ مِّنۡ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَۗ يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلۡيُسۡرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلۡعُسۡرَ وَلِتُكۡمِلُواْ ٱلۡعِدَّةَ وَلِتُكَبِّرُواْ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمۡ وَلَعَلَّكُمۡ تَشۡكُرُونَ

i50kN4Wmy-8.title: Make It the Best Ramadan of Your Life
i50kN4Wmy-8.one_line: First pre-Ramadan khutbah: why Ramadan matters, five reasons for fasting in Al-Baqarah, and six steps to prepare in the coming days.
i50kN4Wmy-8.summary: Opening his pre-Ramadan series, he calls Ramadan his dearest friend and argues that almost every lasting repentance he knows of was anchored in it; without it, Muslims' state would be very different. His motto is to make this the best Ramadan of your life, an intention that counts even if you do not live to see it. He notes that fasting in many religions marks purification before a new stage, and Ramadan is a thirty-day boot camp to turn a new page. Its key lesson is that what you want and what you need differ: the self is a black hole of desire, yet you go without lunch for a month and are fine. He then draws five reasons for fasting from 2:183-185: taqwa as keeping yourself in check, fasting being good for you (so do not overeat at night), ease understood only through hardship, glorifying Allah for guidance, and gratitude, which he defines as action that serves others. In the second khutbah he gives six preparations: enter with a clean heart by repairing broken relationships, delete distractions, write a private list of sins to repent from, prepare a dua list, plan sleep and taraweeh so you stand until the end, and choose new acts of worship.

outline.heading: Opening
A season of return; Ramadan, his best friend
outline.gist: The fasting verses of Al-Baqarah will be recited on every minbar in the coming weeks: as the season nears, all Muslims turn back to Allah and prepare for the same event. Ramadan is the friend he loves most; however exhausting, nothing comes close to its baraka.

outline.heading: Lasting repentance is anchored in Ramadan
outline.gist: He knows of no real, sustainable repentance or change of direction, historically or personally, that was not anchored somehow in this month. Allah designed it that way.

outline.heading: Every year, by design
outline.gist: It comes every year, over eight percent of your life, moving through the seasons so you can keep finding your way back. Imagine your spiritual progress if it came only every few years.

outline.heading: Why Islam keeps growing
outline.gist: Ramadan is a major reason Islam still exists and grows. Groups worldwide try to turn it into a month of eating and TV, but Allah opens His doors, closes the Fire, restrains the devils and calls you, and most respond in some way.

outline.heading: Is this month for you?
outline.gist: Ask yourself honestly: are you far from where you want to be, do you believe you could be closer to Allah? If so, this month is designed for you. Do not be afraid of Ramadan; it is the opportunity of a lifetime.

outline.heading: Motto: the best Ramadan of your life
outline.gist: Make this intention every year, since you do not know whether there will be another Ramadan, or even whether you will reach this one; a sincere intention counts even if you do not.

outline.heading: He did more every year
outline.gist: The Prophet practised this rather than saying it: every Ramadan he went a step further and did something he had not done the year before, knowing the value of living another Ramadan.

outline.heading: Fasting as purification before a new stage
outline.gist: 2:183, prescribed as for the nations before you: almost all religions fast, usually before a life-changing event such as coming of age, war or a new season, symbolising purification. It is no different for us: after eleven months of shortcomings, thirty days to purify yourself.

outline.heading: A thirty-day boot camp for a new start
outline.gist: No food all day, prayer all night, then a fresh beginning: Allah deals with you anew and the embarrassing mistakes are let go, as if the relationship were new.

outline.heading: What you want is not what you need
outline.gist: The self is almost infinite in its desires; the more you feed it the hungrier it gets, like a growing black hole, while what you actually need is very little. Allah proves it rather than having it preached.

outline.heading: Thirty days without lunch, and you are fine
outline.gist: The lunch hour feels sacred, yet you give it up for thirty days and nothing happens: it was a luxury. Would fasting at night while asleep not be easier? No, you fast during the day.

outline.heading: Fasting by day: trained by Allah Himself
outline.gist: He imagines the companions first hearing of daytime fasting, like non-Muslims today asking 'not even water?'. The answer: I am being trained and purified by Allah so I stop rolling in the mud.

outline.heading: Reason one: taqwa
outline.gist: From the fasting verses he draws five reasons. The first, the goal of all worship, is taqwa: keeping yourself in check by asking before every word or deed how it will affect you later, knowing Allah is watching.

outline.heading: Taqwa is built on discipline
outline.gist: Ramadan builds that discipline: you wake fully for suhoor, eat, then go hungry and thirsty all day. Stop planning meals to avoid feeling it; water and dates, and be hungry.

outline.heading: Proof that you can be better
outline.gist: Feeling the hunger shows you need less than you consume. On the Day of Judgment Ramadan is hard to get around: for thirty days you proved you could be a better human being, so you have no excuse afterwards.

outline.heading: Reason two: fasting is better for you
outline.gist: 2:184: fasting is good for you financially, socially and physically; you are supposed to lose weight. Do not turn Ramadan into overeating at night or live for iftar; it is about consuming less. The ill are a different matter.

outline.heading: Reason three: you cannot know ease without hardship
outline.gist: 2:185: Allah wants ease for you, so why thirty days of fasting? Because nothing can be defined without its opposite: life is valued because of death, a flavour because of its opposite, wealth because of a time without it.

outline.heading: Hunger puts your problems in perspective
outline.gist: You fast by choice while others go hungry by necessity, and it makes you compassionate. Stress, deadlines and family disputes become small next to hunger; zoom out and appreciate what you have.

outline.heading: Reason four: glorifying Allah for His guidance
outline.gist: So that you complete the days and glorify Him for guiding you. Part of fasting is ritual: no one on earth but Allah could tell you to give up food and drink, your most basic instincts, and you obey because He is your Lord.

outline.heading: Reason five: gratitude that becomes action
outline.gist: Gratitude is not a feeling but a force that moves you to use what Allah gave you in service of those less fortunate. The hadith that provision increases in Ramadan: not your paycheck, but your perception of how much you have.

outline.heading: Interlude
Preparation one: enter with a clean heart
outline.gist: Plan for the month. In the next ten days repair broken relationships and remove grudges from your heart and others'. Knowledge of the exact Night of Decree was lifted because Muslims quarrelled. Forgive and ask forgiveness; you cannot be more generous than Allah, who returns what you offer others.

outline.heading: Preparation two: remove distractions
outline.gist: Plan how to remove from your day what will keep you from enjoying Ramadan: the phone, too much social media, TV, certain places and habits, and find alternatives. Invest and you will enjoy prayer, Quran and gatherings of dhikr more than anything; young people should go home and start deleting.

outline.heading: Preparation three: a private repentance list
outline.gist: List the sins you still love and want out of your heart by the end of the month. It will not happen organically; Ramadan gives your day and night a system that lowers the chance of sinning. Keep the list to yourself.

outline.heading: Preparation four: a dua list
outline.gist: The Sahabah prepared and memorised what they would ask Allah before Ramadan, their fears and hopes, and kept it private. Even if you do nothing else, do this one.

outline.heading: Preparation five: plan your worship
outline.gist: Plan work, sleep and taraweeh: where you will pray, how you will follow the imam's recitation through the whole Quran, when you will nap.

outline.heading: Stand until the imam finishes
outline.gist: Young people pray a few rak'ahs and leave; you stand longer in line for a burrito or a driver's licence. If tired sit, if more tired lie down, but stay, because you want something from Allah; walking away says you do not care whether He gives it.

outline.heading: If not now, when?
outline.gist: Waiting for retirement, graduation, a job or grown children is an illusion: nothing gets easier, everything gets more complicated. All you have is now; show Allah your desire and He will give you what you did not imagine.

outline.heading: Preparation six: start neglected acts of worship
outline.gist: Choose acts of worship you have not done in a long time and jump-start them in Ramadan so they become habits. The Prophet was at his most generous and giving in Ramadan and put in his greatest effort then.

outline.heading: Recap of the six preparations
outline.gist: A clean heart and repaired relationships, a repentance list, a dua list, removing distractions, a plan for worship, and new acts of worship.

outline.heading: Outro

6iUdesDwe_g.title: Pre-Ramadan Halaqah 3: A Ten-Point Plan for Ramadan
6iUdesDwe_g.one_line: Fasting as a source of strength rather than a burden, then a ten-point spiritual plan for making this the best Ramadan of your life.
6iUdesDwe_g.summary: He argues that a Ramadan without a plan slips away, and that the mindset behind fasting is often backwards: people do things despite fasting, when they should do them better because of it. Fasting trains the body, like the liver relearning to draw on its own stores, to find energy within; the companions survived on date pits, so the question is never whether we can do more, only whether we choose to. He urges people to fast as if they had just accepted Islam, warning that societies decline when their founding values become hollow shells, as he believes freedom has in the West and as fasting has become mere night-time feasting. Inside each person is a black hole of greed that only connection with Allah fills, and Ramadan proves we are happier eating and sleeping less. His ten points: perfect your intention and aim for your best Ramadan; fast with excellence so the fast is accepted; enjoy and live with the Quran through a daily portion; keep daily remembrance; invest in congregational prayer, especially the young; learn something every day; repair relationships before the month; serve others as the way to serve Allah; learn dua as an ongoing conversation; and worship Allah by planning.

outline.heading: Opening
Without a plan the days slip away
outline.gist: Each person needs a personal plan for what they want spiritually from Ramadan, or they find themselves at day sixteen having achieved nothing.

outline.heading: Lessons of the lockdown Ramadans
outline.gist: Leading prayer to two or three people and a camera in empty centres showed how much the blessing of congregation and togetherness is worth; people now value coming together more.

outline.heading: Because of fasting, not despite it
outline.gist: Just as prayer is meant to keep us from wrong rather than be an obstacle, fasting should make us better mannered, more careful with gaze and tongue, and better at our work.

outline.heading: Fasting as purification: doing more with less
outline.gist: Fasting is cleansing, not suffering: it decreases consumption while increasing energy, and humans function best doing more with less.

outline.heading: Ramadan makes strong people
outline.gist: He cites the saying that hard times make strong people and easy times weak ones; Ramadan builds the discipline to stay strong in easy times and make times easier for those who follow.

outline.heading: Gluconeogenesis: finding energy within
outline.gist: After hours without food the liver, like a doctor dusting off a procedure he has not done in years, relearns to draw on stored energy; fasting forces us to find what we need from inside rather than outside.

outline.heading: The companions and the date pits
outline.gist: Companions on an expedition sucked on date pits with water for a day and only realized their value when even those ran out; we can survive on very little, and our potential is greater than we think.

outline.heading: Capability is proven; the rest is choice
outline.gist: Thirty days of fasting prove we can do more with less, so failing to do more is a choice, and we must be honest with ourselves about why.

outline.heading: Fast as if you just accepted Islam
outline.gist: Those raised in the faith fast out of habit without knowing why; habit is good only when the meaning and the One being obeyed stay in view.

outline.heading: Hollow values mark a declining society
outline.gist: Societies rise on deeply held values and fall when those values shrink to skeletons; Islam was built on five pillars, fasting among them, so a hollow fast signals decline.

outline.heading: The Prophet ran to prayer when distressed
outline.gist: Whenever he was upset or afraid he stood in prayer, yet few of his followers do this, because prayer has become mechanics without meaning.

outline.heading: Freedom reduced to a shell in the West
outline.gist: He believes the Western value of freedom of thought, faith and practice has shrunk to a freedom to offend, so real freedom is being lost.

outline.heading: Reclaiming the meaning of fasting
outline.gist: Fasting has been reduced to overeating at night; an ummah that fasts a month every year should be the most persevering, least consuming and most ambitious of nations.

outline.heading: The black hole inside us
outline.gist: Like a black hole, the greed of the nafs devours everything thrown at it, food, wealth, travel, and is never satisfied; only connection with Allah closes it.

outline.heading: Eat less, sleep less, be happier
outline.gist: We do not live to eat; Ramadan shows that with less food and less sleep we are more fulfilled than at any other time of year.

outline.heading: Chasing the mirage
outline.gist: People running after the next possession or trip are like the disbeliever chasing a mirage who finds no water, only Allah waiting to settle his account; Ramadan quiets that greed.

outline.heading: Point one: know why you are fasting
outline.gist: Nothing built without sincere intention lasts or is accepted; before Ramadan, decide what you want from it, write it down, and return to it when distracted.

outline.heading: Be obsessed with your intentions
outline.gist: Muslims today care too little about intention; there is no quick fix, but noticing that your intention is impure is the first step of a long process of monitoring and correcting.

outline.heading: Intend the best Ramadan of your life
outline.gist: No one knows whether they will see another Ramadan, or even reach this one, so resolve to surpass every previous year.

outline.heading: Hard circumstances make it count
outline.gist: The Ramadans he remembers are the exam years, shivering at a bus stop at six in the morning after Fajr; hardship is a reason to make the intention, not to lower it.

outline.heading: Point two: fast with excellence
outline.gist: Sin does not invalidate the fast but endangers its acceptance; fasting puts a buffer between you and haram, so fast with eyes, ears, tongue, hands and feet.

outline.heading: Fasting that earns only hunger
outline.gist: Some will find nothing recorded but thirty days of hunger and thirst. Fasting well is the most important act of the month, more than abundant prayer while mistreating people.

outline.heading: Guard your environment
outline.gist: Fasting with excellence means thinking about where and with whom you spend time, and avoiding places that make wrongdoing likely.

outline.heading: Point three: Ramadan is the month of the Quran
outline.gist: Scholars say Ramadan's status comes from the Quran's revelation in it; the one verse naming the month defines it by the Quran before mentioning fasting.

outline.heading: Close the gap with the Quran
outline.gist: The Quran is the Prophet's legacy, the one thing he made sure would be preserved; if you do not enjoy it you are off course, and every masjid activity exists to clarify Allah's words.

outline.heading: Recite, listen and learn one surah
outline.gist: Recite, memorize, follow the tarawih recitation and attend lessons on meaning; if language or time is a barrier, learn one surah deeply this month.

outline.heading: Keep a daily portion of Quran
outline.gist: The Prophet had companions keep a daily hizb and make it up the next morning if missed; read a juz a day in Ramadan, then keep a baseline of a page or half a page, with reflection and practice.

outline.heading: Point four: a daily wird of remembrance
outline.gist: Ramadan's schedule, around suhoor and between iftar and Isha, makes it the easiest time to start a daily dhikr that lasts beyond the month.

outline.heading: Point five: pray in congregation as much as possible
outline.gist: At home, school or work, with family or roommates, and at a masjid that completes the Quran, staying until the end.

outline.heading: Repair a prayer gone mechanical
outline.gist: Hundreds of rakahs in a month will improve your prayer; treating salah as rote movements is almost criminal, and with shaytan chained only the nafs stands in the way.

outline.heading: No excuses for the young
outline.gist: He accepts no excuse from young people for missing tarawih unless they prove they are busier than him; tired feet are the point, because those nights build lifelong discipline.

outline.heading: The young man asleep in sujud
outline.gist: During a long last-ten-nights prayer years ago, a youth stayed down through several prostrations and toppled over asleep when nudged; that is the effort he expects.

outline.heading: Perfect the daily prayers first
outline.gist: Tarawih means little if Fajr is slept through; the obligatory prayers, in congregation where possible, come first.

outline.heading: Point six: learn something every day
outline.gist: The mind works better while fasting; commit to daily lessons at the nearest masjid or online, and keep at least ten minutes a day after Ramadan, because Muslims are lifelong learners.

outline.heading: Interlude
Showing up matters more than remembering
outline.gist: We forget nearly everything we hear, but the commitment of sitting to learn, even through boring lessons, stays with us and brings wisdom through the month's blessing.

outline.heading: Point seven: revive relationships before Ramadan
outline.gist: Repair ties with parents, relatives and friends you wrongly cut off; entering Ramadan with a grudge is condemned, and the month gives a natural reason to call.

outline.heading: Allah cares how you treat people
outline.gist: Reviving the relationship with Allah includes reviving ties with family, letting things go and forgiving, since life is too short for grudges.

outline.heading: Point eight: a servant must be of service
outline.gist: His only title is servant of Allah, and since Allah cannot be served directly, we serve Him by serving others.

outline.heading: Small ways to serve; selflessness pays later
outline.gist: A soup kitchen, holding the masjid door, tutoring, teaching young relatives Quran; service is ultimately self-serving, a short selflessness cashed in later.

outline.heading: Point nine: dua is a continuous conversation
outline.gist: Dua is not asking until you get something; it is speaking to Allah constantly about fears, hopes, ambitions and struggles.

outline.heading: Take your pain to Allah first
outline.gist: No human fully understands or carries your pain; going to people before Allah humiliates you, though seeking support from family and professionals afterwards is right.

outline.heading: Dua comes from knowing who you address
outline.gist: Dua cannot really be taught; it clicks when you realize He sees and knows everything and you drop the pretence.

outline.heading: Start from the first night; find your heart
outline.gist: Make dua at every iftar and in sujud, and use Ramadan to dig your heart out from under the clutter and speak from it.

outline.heading: Point ten: worship Allah by planning
outline.gist: Islam has no New Year's resolutions; Ramadan is when you plan who you will become, and planning is intention by another name.

outline.heading: Outro

psk8A_-tzBc.title: Pre-Ramadan Halaqah 1: The Bounties of Ramadan
psk8A_-tzBc.one_line: The five bounties Ramadan offers, plus a bonus, explained through the Salman hadith so listeners can build a Ramadan plan around them.
psk8A_-tzBc.summary: Ahead of building a Ramadan plan, he lays out what Ramadan actually offers, starting from the long sermon narrated by Salman. Ramadan is the month of muwasat, easing others' pain, because fasting from lawful food pushes our red line further from the haram and turns hunger into appreciation and compassion; provision increases through gratitude, not income. He then lists five bounties to memorize. First, forgiveness of all past sins through fasting, night prayer or Laylat al-Qadr, and better still Allah's pardon that erases the record entirely; he urges everyone to write a tawbah list. Second, freedom from the Fire, granted nightly to those who strive hardest, which Allah never revokes. Third, immense reward: fasting's reward is uncounted, voluntary deeds equal obligatory ones and obligatory deeds are multiplied seventy times, all for about an hour and a half a night that most people already give their phones. Fourth, Laylat al-Qadr, better than a lifetime, kept hidden so that the sincere commit all ten nights, and a prompt to ask what moment of your life will outweigh its length. Fifth, accepted dua, especially at iftar, with Ramadan as the month for learning to speak with Allah. As a bonus, Allah boasts of fasting servants to the angels. He warns that whoever leaves Ramadan unforgiven is truly deprived.

outline.heading: Why you need a Ramadan plan
outline.gist: Ramadan is the high season of the year; without knowing what you want from it you leave with little, so first learn what it offers.

outline.heading: The Salman hadith and its authenticity
outline.gist: Its chain is disputed, but every sentence but one appears in authentic narrations, and his teachers were comfortable narrating it.

outline.heading: Reading the hadith of Salman
outline.gist: A month with a night better than a thousand months, fasting obligatory and night prayer encouraged, voluntary deeds counted as obligatory and obligatory deeds multiplied seventy times, a month of patience and compassion.

outline.heading: Muwasat: easing another's pain
outline.gist: Muwasat is more than compassion: it is feeling the need to alleviate someone's pain and being a shoulder for them.

outline.heading: How provision increases without more money
outline.gist: Ramadan does not raise your income; fasting and reflecting on it changes how you see what you have.

outline.heading: Fasting from halal pushes the red line from haram
outline.gist: Giving up lawful food, drink and intimacy moves you further from the forbidden; looking at or saying haram while fasting makes no sense.

outline.heading: Shaytan's millimetre nudges
outline.gist: Over years Shaytan moves us slowly toward haram; Ramadan resets where we stand and should carry over afterward.

outline.heading: Hunger as a lens for gratitude and compassion
outline.gist: Hunger shrinks our first-world problems, makes the same bank balance feel like plenty, and softens us toward those who truly lack food.

outline.heading: Five bounties to build your plan on
outline.gist: You cannot plan without knowing what Ramadan brings to the table; memorize its five bounties.

outline.heading: Bounty one: forgiveness of sins
outline.gist: The most important offer is a clean slate; the believer sees his sins as a mountain over his head, the hypocrite as a fly.

outline.heading: Three routes to full forgiveness
outline.gist: Fasting, praying every night, or standing Laylat al-Qadr with faith and hope of reward each wipe out past sins.

outline.heading: Forgiveness versus Allah's pardon
outline.gist: Forgiveness leaves the sin greyed out in your book to be read; pardon ('afw) deletes it as if it never happened.

outline.heading: A rare, limited-time offer
outline.gist: Like an accepted Hajj, Ramadan offers removal of everything, and by the companions' standard many of our best deeds would count as sins.

outline.heading: A fresh start only Allah can give
outline.gist: People can forgive but never forget; Allah offers to start over as if the bad never happened and never ask about it.

outline.heading: Prepare a tawbah list
outline.gist: Write down the behaviours you must repent from and read them; it takes self-honesty, and he does it every year.

outline.heading: Bounty two: freedom from the Fire
outline.gist: Almost unique to Ramadan and Arafah, Allah frees people from the Fire every night and in whole groups in the last ten.

outline.heading: Unseen shackles falling away
outline.gist: Picture the shackles binding us to punishment dropping off, sparing you even the sound of Jahannam when it is paraded.

outline.heading: Once freed, never returned
outline.gist: Allah does not take back what He gives; you will still sin, but you will always find your way back, and be spared the worst verdict.

outline.heading: Ask for it every night and never joke about the Fire
outline.gist: Do not be present when Jahannam is brought forth and every nation falls to its knees in fear.

outline.heading: Allah chooses those who try hardest
outline.gist: It is not a lottery; He looks at who cares most and strives for themselves and their families.

outline.heading: Bounty three: uncounted reward for fasting
outline.gist: Every deed has a set reward except fasting, which Allah rewards Himself; on the scales its line is blank because it cannot be numbered.

outline.heading: No mammal fasts unless Allah commands it
outline.gist: A healthy animal always eats food in front of it; humans refrain only because Allah told them to, so treat fasting with reverence.

outline.heading: Obligatory deeds come first
outline.gist: Nothing draws one closer than the obligatory; one Ramadan fast outweighs a lifetime of voluntary fasts, though voluntary deeds earn Allah's love.

outline.heading: Fast with every limb and never miss Isha
outline.gist: Fast with your tongue, eyes and mind; even when exhausted, pray Isha, since obligatory prayers in Ramadan count seventy times.

outline.heading: Just an hour and a half a night
outline.gist: People spend more than that on their phones daily; Shaytan makes it feel like Everest, but the reward makes it a remarkable deal.

outline.heading: Bounty four: the Night of Status and the Quran
outline.gist: Laylat al-Qadr is when the Quran descended, making Ramadan the month of directly reconnecting with Allah's book.

outline.heading: The first revelation in the cave
outline.gist: Jibril entered without warning and squeezed the Prophet until he thought he would die, commanding him to read.

outline.heading: A world without that night
outline.gist: Many nights could vanish from history unnoticed, but removing that one would change everything.

outline.heading: Better than a thousand months: quality over quantity
outline.gist: A thousand months is a long human lifetime; what matters is what you did with your life, not how long you lived.

outline.heading: Revealed before Ramadan was prescribed
outline.gist: Surat al-Qadr came years before the first Ramadan, asking believers what moment of theirs would be worth a lifetime.

outline.heading: Why the night was hidden
outline.gist: Two Muslims disputing made the Prophet forget its date; Allah kept it hidden so the sincere commit all ten nights.

outline.heading: Every good deed that night outweighs a lifetime
outline.gist: Picture the scales plunging as each kind word, recitation or reconnected tie is multiplied by eighty-three years.

outline.heading: Competing with long-lived nations
outline.gist: Companions worried they could not match nations living centuries; with a median lifespan then around 37, Allah gave them a night better than a lifetime.

outline.heading: Ten Ramadans, ten lifetimes, and the mid-month dip
outline.gist: Attendance surges, sags through the middle and rises late; stick to your plan to the end and arrange life around Ramadan.

outline.heading: Bounty five: accepted dua
outline.gist: Allah answers directly that He is near; every fasting person has an unrejected dua at iftar, and Ramadan is the month of dua.

outline.heading: Dua as a skill and an ongoing conversation
outline.gist: Learn to speak openly and humbly to Allah; the early generations wrote their duas months before Ramadan and memorized them.

outline.heading: Use the iftar moment and never hang up
outline.gist: At iftar turn to Allah with what aches most, and keep the line open beyond Ramadan.

outline.heading: Bonus: Allah boasts of His fasting servants
outline.gist: Allah shows the angels His servants who go hungry by day and stand at night, making them witness His forgiveness.

outline.heading: Gates opened, devils chained, the truly deprived
outline.gist: With the devils chained you have no one to blame for mistakes; whoever misses Ramadan's bounty is truly deprived.

outline.heading: Jibril's dua against one who leaves Ramadan unforgiven
outline.gist: The Prophet said amin to Jibril's dua against a servant who passes Ramadan without being forgiven, since forgiveness is so easy to reach.

outline.heading: Bring your best to Ramadan
outline.gist: Allah watches His servants compete for His mercy, so show Him the best of who you are.

outline.heading: Outro

2:185.ar: شَهۡرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ هُدࣰ ى لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَٰتࣲ مِّنَ ٱلۡهُدَىٰ وَٱلۡفُرۡقَانِۚ فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ ٱلشَّهۡرَ فَلۡيَصُمۡهُۖ وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوۡ عَلَىٰ سَفَرࣲ فَعِدَّةࣱ مِّنۡ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَۗ يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلۡيُسۡرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلۡعُسۡرَ وَلِتُكۡمِلُواْ ٱلۡعِدَّةَ وَلِتُكَبِّرُواْ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمۡ وَلَعَلَّكُمۡ تَشۡكُرُونَ
2:185.en: The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance, and the Criterion (of right and wrong). Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you; and (He desireth) that ye should complete the period, and that ye should magnify Allah for having guided you, and that peradventure ye may be thankful

5QvjF6fBAQQ.speaker_note: his usual voice and style; recalls what his own teachers taught him about adab with Allah; no other speaker named
5QvjF6fBAQQ.title: A Ramadan Plan
5QvjF6fBAQQ.one_line: Pre-Ramadan khutbah on why the month is an unmatched opening for forgiveness and a practical plan: intention, fasting well, Quran, salah, dhikr and dua.
5QvjF6fBAQQ.summary: On the eve of Ramadan he reflects that every imam worldwide recites the same verse, a sign of Allah drawing billions to Him. The month opens Paradise, closes Hell and chains the devils, which he frames as a thirty-day truce to repair the holes in your inner defences. Forgiveness and freedom from the Fire are offered every night on merit, so the truly deprived person is the one who leaves Ramadan unforgiven, usually because they did not want it enough. Good manners with Allah mean valuing what He offers. He argues that failing to plan for something you know is coming shows disrespect, citing the early Muslims' year-long preparation, and says Ramadan recharges a heart running on one percent. His plan: perfect your intention before the month; fast with excellence by keeping eyes, ears and tongue from haram rather than only food; reconnect with and enjoy the Quran; invest in salah by eating lightly and committing to the full taraweeh at the nearest masjid; set a daily dhikr amount; and learn to talk to Allah in dua. He calls people to make this the best Ramadan of their lives, to support one another, and to commit to the masjid nearest home every night instead of fading mid-month.

outline.heading: Opening
Every imam recites the same verse
outline.gist: 2:185, the month the Quran was sent down as guidance, is being recited in tens of millions of khutbahs this week. Who but the King of kings can draw the hearts of billions to Him as the new crescent approaches?

outline.heading: You already know what to do
outline.gist: There is nothing new to say on the minbar: everyone knows what they should do in the next thirty days. Still, take a moment to enjoy what Allah presents, as the Prophet did when he spoke at the start of Ramadan.

outline.heading: The gates of Paradise open
outline.gist: All the gates of Paradise are opened: as the scent of bakhoor drifts out of an open room, something comes out of those gates, which is why Ramadan feels unexplainably special. The gates of Hell are closed and the devils shackled.

outline.heading: Iblis and the thirty-day truce
outline.gist: Your sworn enemy refused to honour Adam and vowed to lead his children like a bridled horse to prove them unworthy. He is removed for thirty days perhaps because your walls are full of holes: a truce to find and fix the flaws in your inner defences before he returns.

outline.heading: Freedom from the Fire, earned on merit
outline.gist: A caller cries each night: seeker of good, come close; seeker of evil, hold back. Allah frees people from the Fire every night, a state of never being punished, but it is no lottery ticket: it is earned by standing longer, reading more, honest self-examination and full repentance.

outline.heading: The truly deprived one
outline.gist: The Prophet rarely spoke harshly, but did about those who live through Ramadan without being forgiven: the deprived one is not the poor or disabled but the one who gains nothing from Ramadan. May he be humiliated; forgiveness is the easiest thing in the month, and the only reason it is missed is not wanting it.

outline.heading: Adab with Allah: value what He values
outline.gist: Too much TV, too much food, no time: his teachers' first lesson was good manners with Allah, valuing what He values. When He opens His doors you come running; what could matter more than a clean slate and a night better than a lifetime?

outline.heading: A name on the list of Jannah
outline.gist: Ramadan is the one chance to get your name written among the people of Jannah, and once it is there Allah never takes it back; He helps you repent after mistakes and find your way back.

outline.heading: Not planning is disrespect
outline.gist: Life forces many spontaneous decisions, but Ramadan does not jump out at you: failing to plan for what you know is coming shows you did not care. The early Muslims spent months praying for acceptance of the last Ramadan and months praying to reach the next.

outline.heading: A heart on one percent
outline.gist: They arranged their work to travel less in Ramadan. Before Ramadan he feels like a phone at one percent and the month catches him just before he collapses; if you skip it for exams or travel, how do you recharge an empty heart? Of his ten points, pick four or five and commit.

outline.heading: Point one: perfect your intention
outline.gist: Treat the month with reverence and you will never regret it. Nothing counts without intention: thousands of rak'ahs mean nothing if done from habit or culture. Know why you fast and pray, for whom, and what you hope for, and keep returning to it for thirty days.

outline.heading: Point two: fast with excellence
outline.gist: Fasting is Allah moving you away from haram by taking away even the most halal things, food, drink and spouse, for the day.

outline.heading: Hungry and thirsty, nothing more
outline.gist: Giving up halal and then jumping into haram makes no sense. Some who fast gain nothing but having been hungry and thirsty, and that is all that will be recorded for them.

outline.heading: Fasting is for Me
outline.gist: Every deed has a calculable reward except fasting, which Allah rewards personally, because only God can tell you not to eat when you are hungry, the very thing you work all your life to provide.

outline.heading: Eyes, ears and tongue fast too
outline.gist: That a whole month of fasting can come to nothing should send a shiver down the spine. When the stomach fasts, the eyes, ears and tongue should fast from haram; watch your thoughts, words and dealings, and when someone provokes you, say 'I am fasting'.

outline.heading: 'I am fasting' is a reminder, not a threat
outline.gist: It is not a warning that you are about to lose your temper but a reminder to yourself: if I give up food for His sake I will not do what angers Him. Allah does not need us hungry; fasting is meant to purify.

outline.heading: Point three: Ramadan's value is the Quran
outline.gist: Ramadan and the Quran cannot be separated: the month has its status because the Quran was sent down in it. Take the book off the shelf and reconnect with it.

outline.heading: Read it yourself, and enjoy it
outline.gist: Learn to recite, memorise and reflect; this is Allah speaking to you. People like him are relevant only as explainers of what He says. He feels sad for anyone who does not enjoy the Quran, for what they are missing.

outline.heading: Point four: invest in salah; eat less at night
outline.gist: Salah is the most important act of worship. Ramadan is the month of fasting, not overeating: one light meal, a few dates and water, since the night is for regaining energy, not hour-long dinners.

outline.heading: Stand with the imam until he finishes
outline.gist: A huge meal means burping, dozing or leaving after one rak'ah and losing a night of qiyam. Find the masjid closest to home and stand from start to finish. Ask your phone how many hours you give it; we wait longer in line at Wonderland or in traffic. If tired sit, if more tired lie down, but be there.

outline.heading: Teach your kids; a training course
outline.gist: Bring your children to learn to stand, bow and make dua in sujood. Ramadan is a training course: after some 300 prayers in a month you should learn ways to stay focused in Fatiha, sujood and istighfar.

outline.heading: Point five: daily dhikr
outline.gist: Ramadan builds habits: set a daily number of adhkar to keep at a better baseline afterwards; when hungry and slow there is little else to do. The Sahabah all had a daily amount of Quran and dhikr, and the Prophet told them to make up any portion they missed the next day.

outline.heading: Point six: the art of dua
outline.gist: Learn to sit and talk to Allah. Every iftar brings a dua that is never rejected, though not always answered as and when you want. Build a lifelong conversation with Him about your hopes, fears and ambitions, and learn to read the signs in your life.

outline.heading: Make it the best Ramadan of your life
outline.gist: Make it your motto every year; you will fall short, but each Ramadan you do a little better. Wellness matters: Muslims who are not well cannot change themselves, let alone the world.

outline.heading: Here is Ramadan: get well
outline.gist: Allah says: get better, learn your purpose, connect with Me and let forgiveness lift the burden off your back. If his plan is not yours, make your own with a clear objective.

outline.heading: Carry each other; learn to love Ramadan young
outline.gist: We pray together so that on the days one of us is not doing well, another holds his hand through it. Young people above all should learn to love Ramadan: however far you drift, it will call you back.

outline.heading: Commit to the nearest masjid every night
outline.gist: Choose the masjid you can reach every day; all the city's imams offer a beautiful experience. Attendance usually peaks in the first nights, falls like Niagara Falls until the twentieth and climbs to the 27th; that should not be you, if you truly want forgiveness.

outline.heading: Outro

pd72txltS6I.title: Ramadan Imam Preparation Seminar: Voice, Pace and Maqamat
pd72txltS6I.one_line: A recitation coach teaches tarawih imams to manage voice layers, loudness, pace and maqam changes so the recitation serves the listener and the meaning.
pd72txltS6I.summary: Working with trainee imams and live examples, the coach teaches how to carry a long night of recitation. Always begin at the lowest layer of the voice, starting with the opening takbir, and rise gradually, or the voice will tire. When closing a passage before ruku, lower the voice and slow down step by step rather than dropping suddenly or stretching letters artificially. He reviews the three recitation speeds of tajweed, tahqiq, tadwir and hadr, and warns against reading everything at hadr: certain verses, such as the contrast of faces in Surat Al-Qiyamah, Surat Ar-Rahman and the endings of surahs, need a slower pace to hold the congregation. He separates pitch layer from loudness, showing how one verse can be read high or low at either level. On maqamat, he advises mastering one rather than hopping between them, avoiding jarring choices that hurt the listener's ear, and changing layer where a meaning completes or the speaker in a story changes.

outline.heading: Opening
Start at the lowest layer and rise gradually
outline.gist: Begin with the opening takbir at the qarar layer and climb step by step, or the voice tires later in the night.

outline.heading: Closing a passage at lower volume
outline.gist: Reciting the end of Al-Baqarah, the reader lowers his volume while staying in the upper layer, a way to signal the close before ruku.

outline.heading: Ending gradually without stretching letters
outline.gist: A common mistake is ending abruptly; descend gradually and slow down, since slowing makes the descent possible, but never stretch letters unnaturally.

outline.heading: The three speeds of recitation
outline.gist: Tajweed names tahqiq, tadwir and hadr; tarawih is usually read at hadr, but some places call for slowing.

outline.heading: Slowing down at verses that need it
outline.gist: Verses like the faces of the Day of Judgment in Al-Qiyamah, Surat Ar-Rahman and the endings of surahs should be read slowly; congregations notice and appreciate it.

outline.heading: Pitch layer versus loudness
outline.gist: Layer and loudness are separate: the same verse on those who say our Lord is Allah and stand firm can be read in a high layer quietly or a low layer loudly, and the reader controls speed, loudness and layer together.

outline.heading: Moving between maqamat
outline.gist: There is no fixed order of maqamat; frequent hopping strains the listener and sounds forced.

outline.heading: Master one maqam and avoid jarring choices
outline.gist: After an example of tarawih in the style of Sh. al-Dosari in maqam saba, he advises settling into one well-mastered maqam and shows on Surat Ad-Duha how an odd maqam choice hurts the ear.

outline.heading: Change layer where the meaning completes
outline.gist: Shift layer when a meaning is complete or the speaker changes, as when Sulayman's question gives way to the ifrit's reply in Surat An-Naml.

outline.heading: Outro

SaixKIXxPIU.speaker: adnan
SaixKIXxPIU.speaker_note: the masjid's lead imam trains his young prayer leaders; says this is his twentieth year leading prayer and that he is 37
SaixKIXxPIU.title: Ramadan Imam Preparation Seminar
SaixKIXxPIU.one_line: Training for young tarawih imams: intention, purity and dress, reciting Fatiha, takbir timing, pacing, witr dua, handling mistakes, and professionalism in service of the congregation.
SaixKIXxPIU.summary: He trains the young men who will lead tarawih, built on one idea: the imam is there to serve the people behind him, so he removes anything that could distract or unsettle them. That starts with intention, since performing for an audience can ruin both the imam and his Ramadan. The imam takes extra care with wudu, avoids wiping over socks out of respect for other opinions, covers his head and dresses traditionally. He should read Fatiha the same way every time, with a steady flow that calms people, say amin audibly, and use the tone and timing of each takbir to tell people what comes next. Movements and pauses should be measured so the congregation is left wishing for more; he gives timings from twenty years of leading and limits the witr dua to ten or fifteen minutes, opening with praise, avoiding repetition and controversial content, and ending with salawat. He covers prostration of forgetfulness and common slips, and urges composure: pause, listen to the corrector, never restart a verse from its beginning. Mistakes are normal; what he will not accept is lateness, poor preparation or unprofessional dress. He also defends giving sisters a real place in the main hall.

outline.heading: Intention: serve people, don't perform for them
outline.gist: Leading is a service, but an imam can become absorbed in how he sounds and how people perceive him; anyone who feels that happening should talk to him and step back to the rows for a while.

outline.heading: Interlude
The imam's wudu
outline.gist: The imam's purity affects everyone behind him, so he makes a full wudu and does not wipe over socks, since some do not accept that opinion; leading is a trust held for the whole congregation.

outline.heading: Dress: cover the head, dress traditionally
outline.gist: These are sunnahs, not obligations, but an imam should not give anyone reason to feel uncomfortable: a head covering, traditional dress, nothing see-through, no holes in socks, nothing exposed in sujud.

outline.heading: Interlude
Remove distractions instead of arguing
outline.gist: A trainee once prayed with a tiger printed on his back. People fixate on small things, and the imam is there to serve, not to defend himself; the Prophet cared about what people would benefit from.

outline.heading: Fatiha: one system, every time
outline.gist: Recite Fatiha with a clear, unbroken flow and stop at the same places each time; do not improvise new ways until you have mastered them.

outline.heading: A steady Fatiha calms people; say amin aloud
outline.gist: A fixed rhythm eases people into the recitation; he has used two set ways for over twenty years. The imam says amin audibly and does not wait for the congregation.

outline.heading: No pause after Fatiha; make every letter clear
outline.gist: Following the Hanafi view, keep going without a pause after Fatiha, and fix any letter you pronounce badly before Ramadan.

outline.heading: The tone of the takbir
outline.gist: Someone behind you who cannot see should know from the takbir's tone whether you are rising for recitation or sitting to finish; keep it audible and clear.

outline.heading: Timing the takbir to the movement
outline.gist: New imams should finish the takbir as they reach the position so no one overtakes them; the proper sunnah is to say it during the movement and finish near its end, never before moving.

outline.heading: Going down and sitting
outline.gist: Go down quietly, hands or knees first; sit in one of the well-supported positions and avoid the forms with least evidence so no controversy arises.

outline.heading: Ruku: a straight back
outline.gist: Arms extended to the knees and a back flat enough to rest a cup of water on.

outline.heading: Duration: leave people wanting more
outline.gist: We are neither racing nor marathoning; the congregation should always be hoping for a few more seconds, not fewer, and overlong positions exhaust people.

outline.heading: Pacing for an untrained congregation
outline.gist: Most people do not know what to say in long pauses, so do not stand extra time after recitation or linger in tashahhud, but do not rush so much that people wonder whether you finished the salawat.

outline.heading: Timings from twenty years of leading
outline.gist: He has timed it: about seven minutes per pair of rakahs when praying twenty, twelve when praying eight, and ten for the ten plus three prayed at his masjid.

outline.heading: Avoid rushed tarawih; prefer the masjid
outline.gist: Never take part in tarawih rushed through in minutes. Students wanting their own campus tarawih would gain more from joining a masjid, or should pray at home with real recitation rather than empty exercise.

outline.heading: Total length, and telling people the plan
outline.gist: Roughly an hour and a half for the whole night and never under forty-five minutes; tell people the plan before starting, and pray in pairs plus one witr rather than three together.

outline.heading: Witr dua: ten to fifteen minutes
outline.gist: Beginners keep the dua to ten or fifteen minutes; people rarely make dua outside Ramadan, so this is where they learn it.

outline.heading: Model duas on proven ones; stay within bounds
outline.gist: Study the first three nights of his duas from last year and run anything unusual by him; creativity is welcome, but avoid aggressive or controversial content.

outline.heading: Avoid repetition in dua
outline.gist: If you forget what comes next, end rather than repeat; repetition turns people off. Beginners should follow the rules before developing their own style, and he will prompt anyone who blanks.

outline.heading: Open the dua with praise
outline.gist: Begin with hamd, as the evidence supports, rather than a lengthy opening; stick to basics while learning so people are not tired or confused.

outline.heading: Organize the dua; control your emotion
outline.gist: Prepare three or four short sections in advance, keep emotion in check without losing the joy of it.

outline.heading: No tajweed chanting; end with salawat
outline.gist: He is not a fan of reciting dua with tajweed melody, though he will not fault it; always close with salawat and develop your own fixed opening and closing.

outline.heading: When prostration of forgetfulness is needed
outline.gist: A wrong formula on rising needs nothing; standing instead of sitting after two rakahs, or the reverse, needs sujud al-sahw, and starting the surah without the opening dua does not.

outline.heading: Once standing, do not go back down
outline.gist: If you rise past the first tashahhud of a four-rakah prayer, stay standing; but in a two-rakah tarawih you must sit, because a third rakah would invalidate the prayer.

outline.heading: Sahw: make each step clear
outline.gist: Say the salam for sahw clearly so people understand, do not resume reciting afterwards, and stay composed so you can hear the person cueing you.

outline.heading: Interlude
Common slips: first tashahhud and losing count
outline.gist: If corrected after standing, hold your ground and prostrate at the end; if you lose count, do what you think is right and follow the front row's cue.

outline.heading: Recitation speed: keep the rhythm
outline.gist: Slowness is his biggest concern for beginners; read at an understandable but steady pace, since an hour and a half tires people.

outline.heading: Calmness when corrected
outline.gist: Pause, let the corrector speak, fix it and move on; he usually corrects when you take a breath.

outline.heading: Slowness strikes, but tajweed is non-negotiable
outline.gist: One strike for slowness, two and you are out; that never licenses poor tajweed, and weak tajweed means a shorter section.

outline.heading: Pause long enough to hear the correction
outline.gist: The worst pattern is not listening, repeating the mistake, then making a new one while fixated on the first.

outline.heading: People praying ahead of the imam
outline.gist: Rows in front of the imam's position are permissible when not directly before him and when space requires it; only the Hanafis strongly object, and even they allow it in need.

outline.heading: Sisters belong in the hall
outline.gist: Boxing women behind curtains or into side rooms makes them feel disengaged, as surveys of sisters showed; men who object should simply face forward.

outline.heading: Arrive early when you lead
outline.gist: Be in your place before the reminder starts so you are not stepping over people, settled and ready; leading is a service and punctuality is part of it.

outline.heading: Never restart a verse from its beginning
outline.gist: If you stop mid-verse, go back two or three words or carry on; restarting the whole verse bothers everyone. Backups and leaders arrive and leave together, as professionals.

outline.heading: Repeating for effect is not for beginners
outline.gist: Going back to the start just makes you lose breath at the same spot; repeating a moving verse for effect is for experienced reciters, not for now.

outline.heading: The corrector's job
outline.gist: Whoever holds the mushaf must stay focused on where the reader is; the masjid needs an agreed system, and here every error is corrected, even small ones.

outline.heading: Bring positive energy
outline.gist: Starting low in tone is right, but the recitation should carry enthusiasm and love for the Quran so people enjoy it.

outline.heading: Eat lightly before leading
outline.gist: Soup and a drink, not a full meal; a full stomach draws blood to the gut and drains the energy needed to recite.

outline.heading: Mistakes are fine; unpreparedness is not
outline.gist: He made countless mistakes in his early years; what bothers him is coming late, badly dressed or unrevised. One trainee struggles every year with nerves and that is no problem.

outline.heading: Don't look at the people
outline.gist: He used to never look back at the congregation; noticing a particular person tempts you to put on a show, so sit facing forward and let two or two million be the same.

outline.heading: Confidence takes time
outline.gist: He remembers how shaky they all were at first; start in small groups with short surahs and build up rather than beginning on a big stage.

outline.heading: If you blank out
outline.gist: Nervous blanks happen; breathe deeply, listen to the correction until you understand it, and refocus. No one is counting your mistakes.

outline.heading: Recite your portion to someone first
outline.gist: Recite your pages, six at most, to a listener beforehand to find weak spots, and study the fiqh of leading prayer.

outline.heading: Corrections protect you; the reward of imamah
outline.gist: Accept correction, since his role is to support you so no one troubles you later. With sincere intention, leading brings the reward of the act and of serving everyone behind you.

outline.heading: Outro

95N45cndSPc.title: Pre-Ramadan Halaqah 2 (Arabic)
95N45cndSPc.one_line: A Ramadan slogan from Musa's words, then three priorities for the month: a corrected intention, the Quran, and prayer, plus dua.
95N45cndSPc.summary: He proposes Musa's words to his Lord, that he hastened to Him so He would be pleased, as the slogan for Ramadan: rushing toward Allah with effort, giving up sleep to please Him. His first piece of advice is to correct one's intention before the month starts, since no deed is accepted without it; the intention should be built on the five rewards discussed earlier, forgiveness, freedom from the Fire, abundant reward, accepted dua and Laylat al-Qadr, so that when energy flags one can renew it. Ramadan is a noble, brief visitor that people dread and then miss. Second is the Quran: Ramadan's rank comes from the Quran's descent in it, and everything linked to the Quran is raised, Jibril and the Prophet included. He urges a full reading, memorizing a new surah and a daily portion to close the gap with Allah's book. Third is prayer: obligatory prayers in congregation come before taraweeh, and missing Fajr after taraweeh is a disaster. He encourages taraweeh without blaming those unable to attend, explains why the Prophet stopped leading it nightly, asks people to stay until the imam finishes, and challenges young men who would stand for hours at sport. A fourth priority is learning to make dua daily.

outline.heading: A slogan for Ramadan: I hastened to You to please You
outline.gist: Musa hurried ahead of his people to meet his Lord, travelling night and day, and explained he did so to win Allah's pleasure; this is the ideal Ramadan motto.

outline.heading: First: correct your intention
outline.gist: No deed is accepted without a sound intention, which is why hadith collections open with the hadith on intentions.

outline.heading: Build the intention on Ramadan's five rewards
outline.gist: Intend forgiveness, freedom from the Fire, abundant reward, accepted dua and Laylat al-Qadr, and renew that intention whenever energy fades.

outline.heading: Ramadan as a brief, noble visitor
outline.gist: Review what you want from the month; people dread it, then regret its passing and pray to reach another.

outline.heading: Second: the Quran gives Ramadan its rank
outline.gist: Ramadan is honoured because the Quran descended in it; anything tied to the Quran, including Jibril and the Prophet, is elevated.

outline.heading: Practical commitments to the Quran
outline.gist: Complete a reading, memorize a surah you have not learned, keep a daily portion, and renew your bond with the only pure truth in existence.

outline.heading: Third: congregational and obligatory prayers first
outline.gist: Men should keep congregation and everyone should guard the obligatory prayers; praying taraweeh while missing Fajr or Dhuhr is a serious problem.

outline.heading: Encouraging taraweeh without blame
outline.gist: The aim is to inspire, not to shame the tired or sick; the Prophet stopped leading it nightly out of mercy, fearing it would become obligatory.

outline.heading: Stay with the imam until he finishes
outline.gist: Keep to this open door of voluntary prayer, sit if tired, but leave only with the imam unless there is a real excuse.

outline.heading: Young men: show Allah your zeal
outline.gist: A young man who can play football for hours has no excuse; showing Allah slackness while He opens the gates of Paradise is poor manners.

outline.heading: A fourth priority: learning dua
outline.gist: Turn to Allah every day with raised hands; dua is an art that must be learned.

outline.heading: Outro

Qo6bPm8AXbA.speaker: adnan
Qo6bPm8AXbA.speaker_note: teaches his yearly fiqh of fasting session at his masjid; refers to his medical background and to arriving in the city ten years earlier
Qo6bPm8AXbA.title: Ramadan Preparation Seminar: Fiqh of Fasting
Qo6bPm8AXbA.one_line: The rulings of Ramadan fasting, exemptions and expiations, then the sunnahs of suhoor and iftar, fasting from sin, tarawih, zakat al-fitr and Eid.
Qo6bPm8AXbA.summary: Alongside the spiritual push for Ramadan, he wants people to know the rulings well enough to stop worrying over every detail. Intention is required and simply knowing you are fasting suffices. His master rule is that anything intentionally taken in that counts medically as nourishment breaks the fast; from it follow the six invalidators and the agreed list of things that do not, such as brushing, forgetful eating, wet dreams, non-nourishing injections and leftover wudu water. On disputed matters he accepts inhalers and drops but holds that any IV line or suppository breaks the fast, while inviting people to weigh the arguments themselves. A central principle is that bodily health outranks perfecting a ritual, so the ill and frail elderly must not fast if it harms them; they eat discreetly and join iftar. He covers travel, pregnancy, breastfeeding and severe fatigue, making up days before the next Ramadan, and the major and minor expiations. He then turns to the sunnah: a simple late suhoor, eating less, breaking the fast immediately on dates or water, dua at iftar, and fasting from sin, which governs acceptance rather than validity. He closes with tarawih judged by Quran and presence of heart, zakat al-fitr, and one outdoor Eid for the whole community.

outline.heading: Opening
Intention: know that you are fasting
outline.gist: Every Islamic act begins with intention. Schools range from a nightly intention to the Maliki single intention for the month; what matters is awareness that today is Ramadan, which suhoor or Fajr already shows. A voluntary fast, unlike Ramadan, can be started mid-morning.

outline.heading: The general rule: intentional nourishment
outline.gist: Anything taken in intentionally that medicine would call nourishment, or its equivalent, invalidates the fast; every ruling that follows is an application of this rule, like laws under a constitution.

outline.heading: Invalidator: eating and drinking on purpose
outline.gist: Eating or drinking intentionally breaks the fast; forgetfulness is treated separately.

outline.heading: Invalidator: intercourse or its equivalent
outline.gist: Any form of sexual intercourse or its equivalent breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Invalidator: induced vomiting
outline.gist: Deliberately making oneself vomit breaks the fast; unintentional vomiting does not. These six cover nearly every situation people will face.

outline.heading: Invalidator: parenteral nourishment
outline.gist: TPN or a saline IV in the emergency department puts water and nourishment into the body and breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Invalidator: smoking of any kind
outline.gist: Tobacco, shisha, e-cigarettes or any inhaled smoke breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Invalidator: menstruation and postpartum bleeding
outline.gist: Women in their period or the forty days after birth do not fast and make the days up later.

outline.heading: Does not break: brushing and miswak
outline.gist: Brushing is fine if toothpaste and rinse water are spat out; miswak, the Prophet's sunnah, is an even safer option throughout the day.

outline.heading: Does not break: eating forgetfully
outline.gist: Forgetting momentarily keeps the fast valid, but the moment you remember you must spit out what is in your mouth. He recalls someone who forgot through a whole restaurant meal and tea, and jokes that this calls for a geriatric psychiatrist.

outline.heading: Do not interrupt someone eating forgetfully
outline.gist: Let them swallow and then remind them, since the forgetful meal is a gift from Allah.

outline.heading: Does not break: a wet dream
outline.gist: Unintentional pleasure in sleep does not affect the fast; ghusl is needed for prayer. Intentional intercourse is the worst way to break a fast.

outline.heading: Does not break: non-nourishing injections; diabetics
outline.gist: Injections into muscle or under the skin, such as blood thinners, B12 or insulin, do not break the fast, but insulin-dependent diabetics must check with their endocrinologist or family physician whether they can fast seventeen hours and how to adjust doses.

outline.heading: Does not break: water left after wudu
outline.gist: Rinse once properly and move on; do not spit fifteen times over traces left in the mouth.

outline.heading: Does not break: swallowing saliva
outline.gist: Saliva never breaks the fast, even if deliberately collected, though that is disliked; he separates technical validity from fasting with excellence.

outline.heading: Disputed: inhalers
outline.gist: The Prophet's words about what enters the body refer to the esophagus, not the trachea; inhalers, including steroid ones, are a medical need with no nourishment, so he holds they are fine, while noting scholars are split.

outline.heading: Disputed: eye and ear drops
outline.gist: Most schools lean towards invalidation, but he holds that medical drops are like stray wudu water. He gives his recommendation and leaves people free to weigh the arguments for themselves.

outline.heading: Disputed: non-nourishing IV infusions
outline.gist: Even a non-nourishing IV push expands the vascular volume, so he holds any IV breaks the fast; iron infusions and transfusions clearly do. Ask the physician what you are given.

outline.heading: Disputed: suppositories and enemas
outline.gist: Given what medicine now knows about rectal absorption into the venous system, he holds suppositories break the fast, though some scholars say otherwise for fever suppositories or enemas.

outline.heading: Using a bidet does not break the fast
outline.gist: Muslims have always cleaned with water in Ramadan; washing is not absorption the way suppositories are.

outline.heading: Blood transfusion counts as nourishment
outline.gist: A transfusion is the most extreme form of parenteral nourishment and breaks the fast; rare cases should be taken to an imam.

outline.heading: Exemption: illness, and health over ritual
outline.gist: If fasting harms the body it is haram to fast, because bodily wellbeing ranks above perfecting a ritual, as with praying seated when standing harms. Kidney disease, chemotherapy, heart disease or frequent oral medication all qualify.

outline.heading: Elderly parents who insist on fasting
outline.gist: Every year elderly women whose children forbid them to fast come hoping he will allow it; he refuses when fasting would worsen their illnesses, and they go looking for another sheikh.

outline.heading: How the exempt behave
outline.gist: Those who cannot fast take only what they need, privately, and still share the atmosphere of fasting and iftar; a woman on her period should not sit eating takeout in front of everyone.

outline.heading: Exemption: travel
outline.gist: Travel permits breaking the fast but does not require it. There is consensus for stays under four days; Hanafis allow up to two weeks. He discourages using it unless necessary because days are hard to make up.

outline.heading: Exemption: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: A pregnant woman in any trimester or a nursing mother may break the fast, with a different follow-up he explains later.

outline.heading: Exemption: severe fatigue
outline.gist: A roofer fasting nineteen hours under the July sun intends to fast every day and breaks only when he can no longer function, making up the days later.

outline.heading: Syrian refugees under the northern sun
outline.gist: Refugees in northern Scandinavia faced twenty-one-hour fasts; they fast by the sun, break when fatigue becomes unbearable, and make up the days when days are shorter.

outline.heading: Make up missed days before the next Ramadan
outline.gist: Many women let days pile up for years; the days must be made up before the following Ramadan or an expiation is added.

outline.heading: Major expiation: when owed and its order
outline.gist: Owed for breaking the fast by intercourse and most likely by deliberate eating: freeing a slave, then sixty consecutive days of fasting, then feeding sixty, taken strictly in sequence.

outline.heading: Sixty days or sixty meals
outline.gist: Few can fast sixty days without a break; if you honestly know you cannot, move on to feeding sixty people, roughly a thousand dollars.

outline.heading: Both spouses owe it; deliberate eating is disputed
outline.gist: For intercourse both husband and wife owe the major expiation without dispute; for eating out of anger the majority say it applies, so the safe course is to pay it. The minor expiation is feeding one needy person per day.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: the chronically ill
outline.gist: People with lifelong conditions needing regular medication do not fast and pay about twenty dollars a day, ideally up front at the start of Ramadan; a physician and imam can say whether a condition qualifies.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: the elderly
outline.gist: Frailty in old age is an exemption in three of the four schools, and children can pay on their behalf; since age is not an objective number, a physician and an imam should assess it together.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: delaying make-up days
outline.gist: Days not made up before the next Ramadan are still owed and carry a one-time payment per day.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: The expiation is owed automatically, even if days are made up in time, and the husband pays it. He urges pregnant and nursing women not to exhaust themselves.

outline.heading: Bleeding does not break the fast
outline.gist: Only menstrual bleeding counts; heavy blood loss that makes someone ill falls under illness instead.

outline.heading: Suhoor: daily, late and simple
outline.gist: Young people especially should not skip suhoor, but it is not a feast; gallons of water and salty snacks only cause harm.

outline.heading: Ramadan is for eating less
outline.gist: Ramadan is when we live the sunnah of moderate eating: no vessel is worse to fill than the stomach, so a third for food, a third for drink, a third for breath.

outline.heading: Bulking, and how the body adapts
outline.gist: Asked about bulking for the gym, he advises letting Ramadan cleanse the body; after ten to fifteen days the body learns to conserve water, so heavy drinking is a psychological crutch.

outline.heading: Break the fast immediately; stop at Fajr
outline.gist: There is sin, not merit, in delaying iftar to seem stronger. Once the Fajr adhan starts you stop eating, whatever the childhood myth he once argued with his own sheikh about.

outline.heading: Break the fast on dates or water
outline.gist: Fresh dates, then dried dates, then water; keep dates in the house to follow the sunnah.

outline.heading: Dua at iftar
outline.gist: After seventeen hours of fasting in submission, breaking the fast is a moment Allah is pleased with you; ask, and He gives what you hope for or better.

outline.heading: Fasting from sin: acceptance, not validity
outline.gist: Looking at haram does not invalidate the fast but endangers its acceptance. If he knew one deed of his had been accepted he would walk out content, but none of us knows.

outline.heading: Deeds handed back to their owner
outline.gist: Some will have prayers thrown back like dirty laundry, and Allah tells the one who did a deed for others to seek his reward from them.

outline.heading: Every limb must fast
outline.gist: Eyes, ears, tongue, hands and feet must all fast; if you hold back from halal, holding back from haram should be automatic. Saying 'may Allah accept' after prayer reminds us acceptance is unknown.

outline.heading: Tarawih: connection and completing the Quran
outline.gist: The number of rakahs matters very little; what counts is time, commitment, connection and completing the Quran, so find a masjid and voice you love rather than fighting over eight or twenty.

outline.heading: Home or masjid, and why youth need the masjid
outline.gist: Both are valid and many families loved home tarawih during COVID, but in a non-Muslim-majority country children come to love Ramadan through the masjid's gathering, food and prayer.

outline.heading: Interlude
Zakat al-fitr: who pays for whom
outline.gist: Fifteen to twenty dollars a person; the man pays for himself, his wife, his children and a fetus past 120 days, and a father pays for an unmarried daughter.

outline.heading: Paying zakat al-fitr in money
outline.gist: He holds money is valid, as do most scholars today, while respecting those who insist on grain.

outline.heading: When to give zakat al-fitr
outline.gist: It must be given before the Eid prayer; the earlier in Ramadan, the fewer scholars allow it, so the last ten nights are best.

outline.heading: Eid prayer: everyone, outdoors, together
outline.gist: Families once went out with even their animals; Eid is a congregation of everyone, preferably outdoors, ideally one per community, so his masjid will never hold its own Eid prayer.

outline.heading: Outro
